en: A square that looks just as defensible — the king advances instead of retreating. But it abandons the protection of its rook along the way.
Another check, pushing the king even further from its pieces.
The queen grabs the rook, now beyond any protection. With the triangle broken, nothing was left to stop it.

The same protective triangle as against rook and bishop — but even sturdier. The knight defends squares a bishop could never reach: from this root, every White try the oracle tested lands back on a draw, with no exception found.
The triangle holds, even better than with the bishop
The same long-distance check as against rook and bishop.

The king stays bunched with its rook and knight. The difference from the bishop: here, every Black move tested from this crossroads holds the draw, not just this one — the knight covers squares that the bishop, trapped on one colour, could never defend.

Queen versus rook, usually winning material for the queen — except here: an ordinary pawn on the 2nd rank, glued to the king and rook, closes a fortress the queen never breaks through as long as the rook stays on the 3rd rank.
The shuttle that never moves
Leaving the 3rd rank to do better?
The shuttle: g3, e3, g3… The rook never leaves the 3rd rank, and nothing the queen plays changes anything.
Tempting: activate the rook, go hunt the queen. But leaving the 3rd rank abandons all protection — the rook ends up alone in the middle of the board.
Check, and an immediate return to the same protecting rank.
White's king simply tucks itself away from the checks. Verified draw: no Black try the oracle tested from this crossroads ever did better.
The queen gobbles the rook for free. Without the shuttle on the 3rd rank, nothing was left to defend it.

A central pawn on the 2nd rank always loses to a lone queen. A rook's pawn doesn't — if White's king is too far away, Black's king finds permanent shelter in the corner, shuffling a1, b1 and b2, which the queen never breaks.
The king's shuttle in the corner
Grab the pawn with check?
The queen comes to check and push Black's king back — the usual method against a central pawn.

The loop closes: we land right back on the position from two moves ago. Black's king has a two-square shuttle (b1-b2) that the queen never closes on its own, as long as its own king stays too far away to lend a hand.
Another check, from the other side.
Tempting — the pawn falls, and it's check to boot. But the queen lands right next to Black's king, undefended by White's own king (still on b7).
And the king comes back to b2 — exactly the starting position, queen shifted one square. Nothing has progressed.
Black's king gobbles the queen for free. Nothing left on the board but the two kings — a draw, this time for a completely different reason than the corner stalemate.

A queen beats a lone rook — but not by magic: the king must be restricted, harassed without rest, until the rook runs out of safe squares. Count the moves: the full win often takes over twenty, one of the longest conversions in the game.
Relentless harassment
The queen centralises near the black king's box — no rushed check, just a square that shrinks his world.
The king has nothing better: every other square loses faster still.
The first check, from the corner — the queen never gives a check that leaves a useless breathing square.
Another purely restricting move. The rook, meanwhile, has almost nothing to do — that is the whole problem for the weaker side here: all it can do is wait.
The rook moves because something must be played — not because it helps.
The queen crosses the whole board for the next check — her mobility is exactly what a lone rook can never match.
The fruit of the harassment: the rook, short of useful squares from the very start, finally falls — WITH check, leaving no breath of counterplay.
Queen against a bare king: the finish is now mechanical.
Mate. Count them: fourteen white moves from the starting position, not one of them a wasted check — each took something away from Black.
Without pawns, two rooks are usually worth slightly more than a queen — but only if they protect each other. Black's king must get off the rank that separates them, or lose one of the two for free.
The king must leave the rank
Staying on the rank costs a rook
And if the queen grabs anyway?
The same check.

Essential: by leaving the 8th rank entirely, Black's king clears the line between the two rooks. Now a8 and h8 defend each other — the queen can no longer grab one without losing the exchange right back.
A square just as close as g7 — but the king stays ON the 8th rank, wedged between its two rooks instead of letting them communicate.
This time the rank is completely clear — the temptation is costly.
The queen grabs the a8 rook for free — the king, having stayed on the rank, blocks exactly the square the h8 rook would have needed to cross to recapture. And it's check to boot.
The h8 rook recaptures at once along the 8th rank. The queen traded its value for a single rook, and the rook side ends up materially ahead: the coordination paid off exactly as intended.

The black pawn is racing, your king is miles outside the square, your own pawn is about to fall: lost? Réti, 1921: draw — via a path chasing TWO goals at once. The study that taught the world the diagonal costs nothing.
The two-hare diagonal
If the pawn runs: queen for queen
The straight line loses

The ONLY move that holds — and the most implausible on the board: the king stands OUTSIDE the h-pawn's square and will stay outside for one more move. But the g7-f6-e5 diagonal aims at TWO targets: h1 behind the black pawn, and c7 in front of his own. Two half-threats make a whole one.
“Push — he'll have to deal with it.” He deals with it in ONE move — and the race resumes, minus a white pawn.
Still outside the square, still on the two-way diagonal. Black must finally choose: keep running, or stop the c-pawn.
Black attends to the c-pawn — what else? If he pushes (h3) instead, see the other chapter: the white king pushes HIS OWN.
THE point of the study. From e5 the king AT LAST threatens both at once: Kf4 catches the h-pawn, Kd6 walks the c-pawn home. Black has one move to parry each threat — and would need two.
Taking the pawn settles one hare… and frees the other: the white king is now INSIDE the square. Geometry has clawed back three tempi.
Black plays the pure race. So the white king swaps hares:
Stone-cold draw. Go back to the first diagram and count: this king stood FOUR squares outside the square. The straight line would have lost; the diagonal saved him.
…and escorts HIS pawn. Both sides promote — count the tempi: together, to the move.
Queen for queen, with check no less. The study is a draw from end to end — provided you saw, on move one, that g7 led to both goals.
The c-pawn is dead; now draw the h-pawn's square from h8: the white king will never get in.
The queen appears ONE square from the king — the story of the whole ending: a single tempo, always the same one, from move one.

White's king touches both Black's knight AND bishop — it can only capture one, for free. Taking the knight holds the draw; taking the bishop, despite being the right colour for the queening square, loses. The king's speed matters more than the colour of the piece left on the board.
Take the knight, then race the queen down
Take the bishop: one tempo too slow
The right choice. The bishop stays on the board — the right colour for h8, which would seem to favour Black — but White's king heads straight for its own race to the corner.
Seems just as natural — capture the piece closest to the pawn. But this leaves the knight, which doesn't need to escort the pawn step by step: it hops straight to the key square.
White's king glues its path to the pawn's, on the same diagonal.
The king arrives exactly on time on the square that matters: right next to the queening square.
The king gobbles the queen the very instant it appears. Verified draw: White's king's speed, not Black's bishop's colour, decided everything.
The knight wins a precious tempo with check — exactly the tempo White's king was missing in the other line.
The knight covers the queening square from a distance — White's king, now out of the race, can no longer change the result.

Henri Rinck, 1920: three minor pieces against a rook in mid-board, free as the wind. One knight move — and the wind becomes a net: wherever the rook goes, a fork is waiting. Black's dream (trading rook for BISHOP, since two knights cannot mate) will come true on none of the fourteen squares.
The net closes
The rook under the king
The rook on d4
The rook on e7

The only win: the sleeping b1-knight enters the game ATTACKING the rook. The tablebase did the counting for us: fourteen legal replies, fourteen lost positions. And Black's one real hope — giving the rook for the bishop, leaving two mateless knights — is nowhere on the list.
The most stubborn: mid-board air. Note that “attacking” the bishop with …Re1 simply hangs the rook to the king (Kxe1!).
Snuggled against her king, protected by him — the rook thinks herself untouchable:
Central, away from both visible knights… but inside the third actor's fork:
Far from everything, one eye on c7 — the rook offers a trade of HER choosing:
The second lash — the same knight, one square on.
Third. The rook now lives to the rhythm of hooves.
The quiet move in mid-chase: the bishop strips the rook of the long diagonal's central squares. Only the wing is left —
— and the wing has a price: the c7-knight, motionless until now, gives the check that sets up the fork.
Fork: king on e5, rook on a5. Twelve moves from two knights that never left their half of the board.
Might as well snap up a knight on the way.

The rook has fallen WITHOUT ever touching the bishop: bishop and knight remain — and that duo mates (see “The Bishop and Knight Mate”). The whole domination came down to this: the rook was always going to fall, just never for the right piece.
…but the check is a FORK: d5 touches f4 and e3 at once.
Three pieces against a bare king — the bishop still alive, so mate is a formality. First illustration: near the king is not the same as safe.
The c7-knight: e6 hits f4 AND d4.
The king wins a knight back — too late: bishop and knight suffice (see the mating course). Note the constant: Black only ever catches THE KNIGHT back, never the bishop.
Declined: the same d5-square forks the other way — f4 and e7.
Wherever the rook went — e3, d4, e7, e5… — some knight geometry was waiting. That is what domination means: not a combination, a state of the board.
One extra pawn is usually enough for the rook to beat a lone knight. The knight lacks the reach to both hold back the pawn and stay out of the rook and king's combined domination.
The pawn marches, the knight can't keep up
The pawn sets off, escorted by its king.
The pawn keeps advancing — the knight, too far away, can no longer get back in time to block it.

The rook attacks the knight directly, left with no defence at all — Black's king is far too distant to help. The rook + king + pawn combination always overwhelms a lone knight that has to do everything by itself.

"The rook belongs behind the passed pawn" is the Tarrasch rule — but Short-Yusupov (1984) is its classic exception: playing the rook behind the pawn RIGHT AWAY only draws. The king must be cut off first.
Cut the king off before tucking the rook in
The rule applied too soon
Not the "behind the pawn" square — but the right one anyway. The rook cuts Black's king off on the 7th rank before thinking about escorting the h-pawn.
The Tarrasch rule says: rook behind the passed pawn. Played immediately, without cutting Black's king off first, it only draws.
The only way to cause trouble: harass White's king with checks.
The checks are exhausted — Black's rook has no idea left but to come back and watch the h-pawn.
Left to itself far from its protecting pawn, Black's king is pushed back even further — White's rook gains ground before falling back.

Only NOW does the rook reach the "behind the pawn" square — after winning several extra tempi by cutting Black's king off along the way. The same square as move one, but the position around it has completely changed.
Black's king, still free to roam, heads straight for the pawn's zone and neutralises everything. The rule is only a heuristic — the concrete position decides.
King and rook versus king: the mate every player MUST be able to force, no clock burning, no 50-move rule looming. A method in three verbs: cut, approach, shrink.
Cut, approach, shrink
CUT: the rook draws a border the black king will never cross again. He now lives in a four-rank box — and it will only ever shrink.
APPROACH: the rook cannot mate alone, and needs no help holding its rank. So it is ALWAYS the king who does the work.
The king strolls up — the border holds by itself.
SHRINK: the moment the black king steps away, the rook advances one rank. The box loses a floor — he will never get it back.
The check that DRIVES: when the kings stand face to face, the rook check forces the black king towards the edge. Kings face to face first, check second — in that order.
The black king circles inside his box; the white king shadows him, square by square.
One and a half ranks left. Watch the finish closely: it demands one precision — exactly one.
The waiting move that avoids stalemate and confines to the a-file. The black king has two squares left: a1 and a2.
Kings face to face, check along the edge rank: the rook mate's final picture, to know like your own pocket — it is what you aim at from move one.

An extra pawn, an active rook — and yet almost everything White can play only draws. One single principle separates the win from the draw here: cut Black's king off before even thinking about advancing the pawn.
Cut off first, advance later
Pushing before cutting off
The rook settles on the 3rd rank: Black's king can never approach the pawn from the south again. This cutoff, not the pawn itself, decides everything.
Looks efficient — advance the pawn while you're at it. But without a cutoff, it stands undefended.
Black grabs the pawn with check — the only somewhat concrete try. But trading the rook for the pawn leads to a bare king-and-rook versus king, won by anyone who knows the elementary technique.
The king recaptures the rook. What's left — White king and rook against Black's lone king — is just the already-known elementary finale: won, without a shred of doubt.
Black's rook grabs it with check. The pawn is gone, and with it every winning chance — a draw, rook against rook.

Everything “The Opposition” taught you has one exception: the rook's pawn. Here the corner is an unassailable shelter — the weak side heads for h8 and NOTHING can evict him. Provided he runs there at once.
Run to the corner
The detour that loses
Straight for h8, no detours (Ke8 also holds). Against any other pawn this would be lost; against the rook's pawn the corner saves you — provided you get there.
“I'll stay central and see.” One idling tempo and the white king takes the SHOULDER: the road to the corner is cut forever.
Shoulder to shoulder: don't let the white king get IN FRONT of his pawn — his only hope, and even that leads nowhere.
The white king tries the grand tour via f6? Watch the corner suffice.
The one-square fortress. Fix the image: against a rook's pawn, the defending king on h8 can be NEITHER evicted NOR zugzwanged — he shuttles between h8 and g8 until the end of time.
Nothing works: g8 and h8 are equivalent, and White has no waiting move — the rook's pawn has no spare file!
The “winning” push… and it's STALEMATE. The mistake is White's this time: which is why the strong side must know this ending too — so as not to enter it.
The shoulder-charge: White doesn't push the pawn, he blocks the road first. Compare the main line, where f7 was denied to him.
Too late: g8 belongs to White, the pawn simply walks.
Same pawn, same race — but a defending king that left ONE tempo late. The whole ending lived in the first move.

Two connected passed pawns, already well advanced, against a lone rook: it can never watch both queening squares at once, and any flank check just chases it away without stopping anything. Verified from a neutral position — the technique is robust, almost everything wins.
The pawns outrun the rook
The first pawn advances — Black's rook can't blockade it without letting the second one run.
